REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX(the male claimant), his spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the female claimant) and their minor child XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor claimant), all citizens of Colombia, are claiming refugee protection on the basis of section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).

[2] The minor claimant and the male claimant are basing their refugee protection claims on that of the female claimant, who has been appointed as the designated representative for her child.
SUMMARY OF ALLEGED FACTS

[3] The facts alleged in the original Basis of Claim Form1 (BOC Form) can be summarized as follows.

[4] In XXXX, the adult claimants had been socially active with organizations assisting XXXX populations such as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXXand XXXX, since XXXX 2016. A few months later, in XXXX and XXXX2016, the female claimant was targeted three times by an unknown individual who was trying to recruit her on behalf of Los Urabenos. The male claimant was targeted in XXXX 2016 after the female claimant went to the authorities and the claimants moved. They once again sought the assistance of the authorities before leaving the city of XXXX for XXXX to rebuild their life. A few months later, in XXXX 2017, the female claimant was once again assaulted and was the victim of a murder attempt. The claimants went to the authorities in XXXX, but in vain. They left for XXXX, where they decided to flee the country, which they did a few days later, arriving in the XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX and claiming refugee protection in Canada at the border the next day. They signed their BOC Forms on May 23, 2017.

[5] In an amendment to their account, the claimants subsequently alleged that on XXXX XXXX, 2017, two men broke into the home of the female claimant's mother to inform her, violently, that they would kill the claimants as a military objective if they ever returned to the country.
DETERMINATION

[6] For the reasons that follow, the panel determines that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" within the meaning of section 96 of the Act nor "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the Act.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[7] In light of the identity documents submitted as evidence, the panel is satisfied as to the claimants' identities.

[8] When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. In the case at hand, as noted by their counsel in his written submissions,2 no significant contradictions were raised during the claimants' testimony, and considerable evidence has been submitted regarding their allegations. The panel agrees. The panel even adds that it has rarely seen a file so well prepared; the claimants went so far as to produce a receipt for the bus trip they took when fleeing XXXX. In fact, nearly all the claimants' allegations are corroborated by documentary evidence. In addition, the factual framework contains all the necessary elements to conclude that there is a prospective risk, as well as an absence of state protection or an internal flight alternative. Faced with a file so well put together, the panel recalls the following words of a Federal Court judge:
... Evidence of a seamless web of diverse events occurring over time and distance, all intersecting propitiously and recalled with clarity and precision, should be viewed with the same caution as testimony which, by reason of multiple inconsistencies on critical issues, does not hold.3

[9] With this caution in mind, the panel sent the Minister a notice under rule 27 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules during its deliberations.4 This notice raised two concerns. First, the panel was concerned by the similarities between the claimants' story and those of claimants in other files. These similarities lay in both the basis of the narratives, in particular the systematic presence in the account of recurring elements such as murder attempts that failed as a result of exceptional circumstances, and incidents that occurred in distant cities where the claimants went to flee their problems. The Minister declined to intervene5 and the panel is therefore disregarding this concern, having chosen not to communicate the content of the other files in question and pursue the matter further.

[10] Second, the panel notified the Minister of a concern raised during the hearing, namely the presence of complaints6 in the claimants' file that are categorized as "inactivo" according to complaint reports filed through the Sistema Penal Oral Acusatorio [oral accusatory penal system] of the Fiscalia General de la Nation (FGN) [office of the attorney general].7 However, the "inactivo" status of these complaints could possibly indicate, according to responses to information requests (RIRs) produced by IRB's research services,8 that an FGN officer has determined that the crime in question did not take place.9 While the Minister also declined to intervene in this regard, the panel remains concerned by the fact that the claimants may be submitting real complaints based on fictitious facts. However, this concern does not have to do with the "inactivo" status of the complaints-the RIRs in question leave too much room for interpretation to draw a satisfactory conclusion in this regard. It also does not have to do with the authenticity of the complaints, as those submitted as evidence10 appear to be authentic. Moreover, the concern does not have to do with contradictions or omissions, as the complaints in question essentially present allegations that are consistent with each other, as well as with the claimants' story as related in the BOC Form and at the hearing. Rather, the panel is concerned about the authorities' and the complainants' follow-up to these complaints.

[11] The above-referenced RIRs report that the decision to close a complaint is usually sent to the complainant by telegram sent to the address that he or she provided. The document i) indicates that the complaint was closed and ii) provides the contact information of the FGN office where the complainant can go to learn the reasons for the decision, and iii) includes an appointment with the date and time to meet with the prosecutor. Also according to the RIRs, during the appointment, the prosecutor will produce the order closing the complaint and explain the reasons for doing so. The complainant receives a copy. In the case at hand, despite the existence of three complaints to the FGN, the only document the claimants produced in this regard is Exhibit C-31 regarding complaint D-22. However, this exhibit does not provide FGN contact information and does not inform the claimants of the possibility of obtaining more information (or even the date and time of an appointment). It also does not specify the report number assigned to the complaint-a unique number by which the complaint can be identified and traced. Moreover, its format is suspicious: the FGN logo is printed twice, one on top of the other, and covers the document date. Asked to comment, the claimants confirmed at the hearing that this document was the one they had received and referred the panel to their counsel in Colombia who was responsible for following up on all the complaints. This counsel stated in writing that the document is authentic and original and was issued by the FGN. He also explains that he met with the prosecutor responsible for the investigation and asked for it to be reopened, but the prosecutor refused because it was impossible to physically identify the perpetrators of the crime. He did not offer a copy of the decision or the order to archive the complaint, nor did he elaborate on what steps he could take to dispute the decision not to reopen the investigation. In short, he provided a vague version that does not inspire confidence in light of the aforementioned RIRs, which describe the rights and recourse available to complainants whose complaints are archived. With respect to follow-up on the other FGN complaints, counsel in Colombia is even more eager for details and essentially merely confirms their inactive status.

[12] The claimants' counsel in Canada observed that they should not be blamed for an unfamiliar legal situation regarding the status of the complaints. Whether or not these complaints are active, the claimants always followed the advice of their counsel in Colombia, who was mandated to represent them regarding their complaints and their protection. The panel informed the claimants of its concerns about the FGN complaints and gave them the time necessary to address these complaints. In the panel's opinion, the explanations contained in the two letters from counsel in Colombia11 do not satisfactorily explain the divergence between what the RIRs report about the complaint process and the situation alleged by the claimants. In light of the credibility problems outlined below, the panel is of the opinion that this divergence is better explained by the fact that the complaints were in fact made but concern fictional events, than by the claimants' version of their story being true and them relying on the good faith of their counsel in Colombia.

[13] In arriving at this conclusion, the panel also relied on the follow-up to their applications for protection made to the National Protection Unit (UNP).12 According to their Colombian counsel, he followed up in person and confirmed that the file was still being processed and that no response had been received as of XXXX XXXX, 2018. The claimants confirmed that they did not take any steps personally, again relying on their Colombian counsel. According to the documentary evidence,13 evaluation of the application by the UNP takes approximately three months and the person concerned receives a decision in writing to inform him or her of whether the application has been approved or denied, and of the protection measures that are to be implemented. In light of the documentary evidence (which presents the strengths and weaknesses of this organization and merits more weight than letters from the claimants' Colombian counsel in the circumstances), the panel finds it improbable that the claimants would have received no response or communication from the UNP in the more than 14 months since they submitted their applications. This is particularly true since the claimants were-and say they still are-reachable via the email addresses indicated on the applications. In the circumstances, the panel therefore concludes that the claimants are hiding the real outcome of their applications for protection to the UNP. This strengthens the panel's conclusion that the claimants made actual requests for protection, but on the basis of fictional facts and likely did so in order to prepare their Canadian refugee protection claims.

[14] In summary, while the panel is aware of the shortcomings in the protection Colombian authorities provide to citizens, including their capacity to investigate criminal offences, the panel is of the opinion that submitting applications for protection in Colombia triggers objective and verifiable measures that have not been demonstrated in this case, and the claimants have not been able to reasonably explain the absence of these measures. Taking into account all the credibility problems noted below, the panel concludes that the claimants have manipulated the Colombian protection system by submitting actual complaints based on fictitious events. It therefore gives no evidentiary weight to the measures taken by the claimants with the Colombian authorities.

[15] Another element undermining the claimants' credibility: their alleged stay of several months in XXXX while fleeing their alleged problems in XXXX. The panel questioned the claimants at length about this stay, given that they allegedly arrived in this city, over 300 kilometres from XXXX, with the intention of rebuilding their life. Living in a new city requires actions that leave traces and that can be documented, beyond the exhibits submitted in evidence prior to the hearing and pertinent to this stay.14 Without going into details, the panel observed that all the evidence submitted (before and after15 the hearing) in this regard is documents it gives no evidentiary weight to in the circumstances, given that they come from sources controlled by the claimants, that they are easy to fabricate or that they present inconsistencies.16 The claimants could not produce any documents that might have merited evidentiary weight (e.g., confirmations of bank transfers that the claimants allegedly received in XXXX from their parents or their own bank statements reflecting ATM withdrawals in XXXX or purchases they allegedly made from businesses in the city). On one hand, they did not keep them (even though they fortuitously kept a hotel invoice and a transportation ticket); on the other hand, efforts to obtain them since have been unsuccessful.17 Rather than elaborate on whether or not these efforts and explanations for the lack of independent evidence to corroborate the claimants' alleged stay in XXXX are reasonable, the panel will turn to a more determinative element, namely the fact that the male claimant was issued a new driver's licence in XXXX during this alleged stay. The male claimant explained that he did not go to the national capital in person to get this document (nor to any other government institution in the country), but that, instead, his father had done so on his behalf. Confronted with the fact that his own presence is required for this according to the documentary evidence,18 the claimant stated that he had never returned to XXXX and that his father had taken the necessary steps. In support of this argument, he used the extension granted by the panel to submit documents after the hearing,19 including a letter from himself asking his father to do this, a statement from his father and a statement from a business indicating that [translation] "it was possible to renew a driver's licence without the presence of the licence-holder via an authorization and with the documents mentioned above, but it is no longer possible after the latest reforms." Note that the male claimant did not produce [translation] "independent and objective" documents from the authorities responsible for issuing driver's licences confirming the possibility of having a driver's licence issued in the circumstances alleged in XXXX 2017. Nor did he submit "independent and objective" documents supporting "the latest reforms" mentioned in the statement from the aforementioned business or the date of these reforms. Moreover, the aforementioned documentary evidence states the following:
Sources indicate that driver's licences for personal vehicles are valid indefinitely. However, the website of the Ministry of Transportation indicates that the holder has to undergo a professional medical exam every six years to prove his or her mental and physical suitability to drive a personal vehicle.
Two sources indicated that a driver's licence can be obtained only in person. The representative of the Secretariat of Transportation and Traffic of XXXX explained that it has to be done in person because an individual has to be fingerprinted and his or her photograph has to be taken.20

[16] This documentary evidence is dated 2013, well before the date when the claimant obtained his new driver's licence in XXXX 2017 (and obviously before the reforms supposedly made thereafter, according to the statement from the aforementioned business). The panel therefore concludes that the documents submitted by the claimant contain false statements fabricated to hide the fact that he was in XXXX in XXXX 2017. The panel therefore gives them no probative value and prefers the objective documentary evidence cited above, given the circumstances. Moreover, the panel concludes, in the circumstances, that the claimants are attempting to mislead the panel by alleging that they lived in hiding in XXXX and feared problems in XXXX.

[17] In this context, the panel also gives no weight to the other documents submitted by the claimants from family members and/or people they may be able to influence.21

[18] In arriving at its conclusions, the panel also took into account other concerns raised at the hearing. In each instance, the claimants gave problematic explanations that led the panel to draw negative inferences concerning the claimants' credibility as a result of these concerns. For example, the claimants stated that the people they feared had identified themselves as the Los Urabeños group. However, this group does not use this name to identify itself, but rather the name Autodefensas Gaitanistas de Colombia (AGC) [Gaitanist self-defense forces of Colombia], according to the documentary evidence.22 Invited to comment on this suspicious allegation, the claimants simply responded that that is how the person identified themself. The panel rejects this explanation, finding it improbable that a member of the AGC would identify themself that way in light of the available documentary evidence.

[19] As a second example, each of the claimants survived in extremis what they described as murder attempts. The male claimant was the first to successfully disarm and flee from an assailant who held a pistol to his head saying he would kill him. The female claimant also had a lucky escape a few months later when she, like the male claimant, was able to hit her assailant, causing him to lose his balance and the gun he had pointed at her. Moreover, the female claimant explained that, while she was fleeing, she was able to observe that her assailant had pointed his pistol at her and tried to fire more than once, but the weapon had jammed. Invited to comment on this rather unbelievable account, she explained that that is what happened, despite the fact that it was dark (the assailant was allegedly under the light of a street light) and she was running at full speed with her child in her arms to get away. The panel finds it improbable that a person fleeing imminent death with a young child in her arms would be able to see that her assailant-who was behind her and from whom she was running away-was pointing a weapon at her, pulling the trigger with his finger and then hitting his weapon as though it was damaged, all by the light of a street light. The panel does not believe the alleged incidents in the circumstances.

[20] For all these reasons,23 the panel concludes that the claimants have not credibly established their story, including the incidents alleged on and after XXXX XXXX, 2016.
Section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Act

[21] In light of its foregoing conclusion, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants have not established that they would face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or the likelihood of a risk or danger set out in subsection 97(1) of the Act.
CONCLUSION

[22] For the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" under section 96 nor "persons in need of protection" under paragraphs 97(1)(a) or (b) of the Act.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX(the male claimant), his spouse XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (the female claimant) and their minor child XXXX XXXX XXXX (the minor claimant), all citizens of Colombia, are claiming refugee protection on the basis of section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the Act).

[2] The minor claimant and the male claimant are basing their refugee protection claims on that of the female claimant, who has been appointed as the designated representative for her child.
SUMMARY OF ALLEGED FACTS

[3] The facts alleged in the original Basis of Claim Form1 (BOC Form) can be summarized as follows.

[4] In XXXX, the adult claimants had been socially active with organizations assisting XXXX populations such as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXXand XXXX, since XXXX 2016. A few months later, in XXXX and XXXX2016, the female claimant was targeted three times by an unknown individual who was trying to recruit her on behalf of Los Urabenos. The male claimant was targeted in XXXX 2016 after the female claimant went to the authorities and the claimants moved. They once again sought the assistance of the authorities before leaving the city of XXXX for XXXX to rebuild their life. A few months later, in XXXX 2017, the female claimant was once again assaulted and was the victim of a murder attempt. The claimants went to the authorities in XXXX, but in vain. They left for XXXX, where they decided to flee the country, which they did a few days later, arriving in the XXXX XXXX on XXXX XXXX and claiming refugee protection in Canada at the border the next day. They signed their BOC Forms on May 23, 2017.

[5] In an amendment to their account, the claimants subsequently alleged that on XXXX XXXX, 2017, two men broke into the home of the female claimant's mother to inform her, violently, that they would kill the claimants as a military objective if they ever returned to the country.
DETERMINATION

[6] For the reasons that follow, the panel determines that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" within the meaning of section 96 of the Act nor "persons in need of protection" within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the Act.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[7] In light of the identity documents submitted as evidence, the panel is satisfied as to the claimants' identities.
Credibility

[8] When a claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. In the case at hand, as noted by their counsel in his written submissions,2 no significant contradictions were raised during the claimants' testimony, and considerable evidence has been submitted regarding their allegations. The panel agrees. The panel even adds that it has rarely seen a file so well prepared; the claimants went so far as to produce a receipt for the bus trip they took when fleeing XXXX. In fact, nearly all the claimants' allegations are corroborated by documentary evidence. In addition, the factual framework contains all the necessary elements to conclude that there is a prospective risk, as well as an absence of state protection or an internal flight alternative. Faced with a file so well put together, the panel recalls the following words of a Federal Court judge:
... Evidence of a seamless web of diverse events occurring over time and distance, all intersecting propitiously and recalled with clarity and precision, should be viewed with the same caution as testimony which, by reason of multiple inconsistencies on critical issues, does not hold.3

[9] With this caution in mind, the panel sent the Minister a notice under rule 27 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules during its deliberations.4 This notice raised two concerns. First, the panel was concerned by the similarities between the claimants' story and those of claimants in other files. These similarities lay in both the basis of the narratives, in particular the systematic presence in the account of recurring elements such as murder attempts that failed as a result of exceptional circumstances, and incidents that occurred in distant cities where the claimants went to flee their problems. The Minister declined to intervene5 and the panel is therefore disregarding this concern, having chosen not to communicate the content of the other files in question and pursue the matter further.

[10] Second, the panel notified the Minister of a concern raised during the hearing, namely the presence of complaints6 in the claimants' file that are categorized as "inactivo" according to complaint reports filed through the Sistema Penal Oral Acusatorio [oral accusatory penal system] of the Fiscalia General de la Nation (FGN) [office of the attorney general].7 However, the "inactivo" status of these complaints could possibly indicate, according to responses to information requests (RIRs) produced by IRB's research services,8 that an FGN officer has determined that the crime in question did not take place.9 While the Minister also declined to intervene in this regard, the panel remains concerned by the fact that the claimants may be submitting real complaints based on fictitious facts. However, this concern does not have to do with the "inactivo" status of the complaints-the RIRs in question leave too much room for interpretation to draw a satisfactory conclusion in this regard. It also does not have to do with the authenticity of the complaints, as those submitted as evidence10 appear to be authentic. Moreover, the concern does not have to do with contradictions or omissions, as the complaints in question essentially present allegations that are consistent with each other, as well as with the claimants' story as related in the BOC Form and at the hearing. Rather, the panel is concerned about the authorities' and the complainants' follow-up to these complaints.

[11] The above-referenced RIRs report that the decision to close a complaint is usually sent to the complainant by telegram sent to the address that he or she provided. The document i) indicates that the complaint was closed and ii) provides the contact information of the FGN office where the complainant can go to learn the reasons for the decision, and iii) includes an appointment with the date and time to meet with the prosecutor. Also according to the RIRs, during the appointment, the prosecutor will produce the order closing the complaint and explain the reasons for doing so. The complainant receives a copy. In the case at hand, despite the existence of three complaints to the FGN, the only document the claimants produced in this regard is Exhibit C-31 regarding complaint D-22. However, this exhibit does not provide FGN contact information and does not inform the claimants of the possibility of obtaining more information (or even the date and time of an appointment). It also does not specify the report number assigned to the complaint-a unique number by which the complaint can be identified and traced. Moreover, its format is suspicious: the FGN logo is printed twice, one on top of the other, and covers the document date. Asked to comment, the claimants confirmed at the hearing that this document was the one they had received and referred the panel to their counsel in Colombia who was responsible for following up on all the complaints. This counsel stated in writing that the document is authentic and original and was issued by the FGN. He also explains that he met with the prosecutor responsible for the investigation and asked for it to be reopened, but the prosecutor refused because it was impossible to physically identify the perpetrators of the crime. He did not offer a copy of the decision or the order to archive the complaint, nor did he elaborate on what steps he could take to dispute the decision not to reopen the investigation. In short, he provided a vague version that does not inspire confidence in light of the aforementioned RIRs, which describe the rights and recourse available to complainants whose complaints are archived. With respect to follow-up on the other FGN complaints, counsel in Colombia is even more eager for details and essentially merely confirms their inactive status.

[12] The claimants' counsel in Canada observed that they should not be blamed for an unfamiliar legal situation regarding the status of the complaints. Whether or not these complaints are active, the claimants always followed the advice of their counsel in Colombia, who was mandated to represent them regarding their complaints and their protection. The panel informed the claimants of its concerns about the FGN complaints and gave them the time necessary to address these complaints. In the panel's opinion, the explanations contained in the two letters from counsel in Colombia11 do not satisfactorily explain the divergence between what the RIRs report about the complaint process and the situation alleged by the claimants. In light of the credibility problems outlined below, the panel is of the opinion that this divergence is better explained by the fact that the complaints were in fact made but concern fictional events, than by the claimants' version of their story being true and them relying on the good faith of their counsel in Colombia.

[13] In arriving at this conclusion, the panel also relied on the follow-up to their applications for protection made to the National Protection Unit (UNP).12 According to their Colombian counsel, he followed up in person and confirmed that the file was still being processed and that no response had been received as of XXXX XXXX, 2018. The claimants confirmed that they did not take any steps personally, again relying on their Colombian counsel. According to the documentary evidence,13 evaluation of the application by the UNP takes approximately three months and the person concerned receives a decision in writing to inform him or her of whether the application has been approved or denied, and of the protection measures that are to be implemented. In light of the documentary evidence (which presents the strengths and weaknesses of this organization and merits more weight than letters from the claimants' Colombian counsel in the circumstances), the panel finds it improbable that the claimants would have received no response or communication from the UNP in the more than 14 months since they submitted their applications. This is particularly true since the claimants were-and say they still are-reachable via the email addresses indicated on the applications. In the circumstances, the panel therefore concludes that the claimants are hiding the real outcome of their applications for protection to the UNP. This strengthens the panel's conclusion that the claimants made actual requests for protection, but on the basis of fictional facts and likely did so in order to prepare their Canadian refugee protection claims.

[14] In summary, while the panel is aware of the shortcomings in the protection Colombian authorities provide to citizens, including their capacity to investigate criminal offences, the panel is of the opinion that submitting applications for protection in Colombia triggers objective and verifiable measures that have not been demonstrated in this case, and the claimants have not been able to reasonably explain the absence of these measures. Taking into account all the credibility problems noted below, the panel concludes that the claimants have manipulated the Colombian protection system by submitting actual complaints based on fictitious events. It therefore gives no evidentiary weight to the measures taken by the claimants with the Colombian authorities.

[15] Another element undermining the claimants' credibility: their alleged stay of several months in XXXX while fleeing their alleged problems in XXXX. The panel questioned the claimants at length about this stay, given that they allegedly arrived in this city, over 300 kilometres from XXXX, with the intention of rebuilding their life. Living in a new city requires actions that leave traces and that can be documented, beyond the exhibits submitted in evidence prior to the hearing and pertinent to this stay.14 Without going into details, the panel observed that all the evidence submitted (before and after15 the hearing) in this regard is documents it gives no evidentiary weight to in the circumstances, given that they come from sources controlled by the claimants, that they are easy to fabricate or that they present inconsistencies.16 The claimants could not produce any documents that might have merited evidentiary weight (e.g., confirmations of bank transfers that the claimants allegedly received in XXXX from their parents or their own bank statements reflecting ATM withdrawals in XXXX or purchases they allegedly made from businesses in the city). On one hand, they did not keep them (even though they fortuitously kept a hotel invoice and a transportation ticket); on the other hand, efforts to obtain them since have been unsuccessful.17 Rather than elaborate on whether or not these efforts and explanations for the lack of independent evidence to corroborate the claimants' alleged stay in XXXX are reasonable, the panel will turn to a more determinative element, namely the fact that the male claimant was issued a new driver's licence in XXXX during this alleged stay. The male claimant explained that he did not go to the national capital in person to get this document (nor to any other government institution in the country), but that, instead, his father had done so on his behalf. Confronted with the fact that his own presence is required for this according to the documentary evidence,18 the claimant stated that he had never returned to XXXX and that his father had taken the necessary steps. In support of this argument, he used the extension granted by the panel to submit documents after the hearing,19 including a letter from himself asking his father to do this, a statement from his father and a statement from a business indicating that [translation] "it was possible to renew a driver's licence without the presence of the licence-holder via an authorization and with the documents mentioned above, but it is no longer possible after the latest reforms." Note that the male claimant did not produce [translation] "independent and objective" documents from the authorities responsible for issuing driver's licences confirming the possibility of having a driver's licence issued in the circumstances alleged in XXXX 2017. Nor did he submit "independent and objective" documents supporting "the latest reforms" mentioned in the statement from the aforementioned business or the date of these reforms. Moreover, the aforementioned documentary evidence states the following:
Sources indicate that driver's licences for personal vehicles are valid indefinitely. However, the website of the Ministry of Transportation indicates that the holder has to undergo a professional medical exam every six years to prove his or her mental and physical suitability to drive a personal vehicle.
Two sources indicated that a driver's licence can be obtained only in person. The representative of the Secretariat of Transportation and Traffic of XXXX explained that it has to be done in person because an individual has to be fingerprinted and his or her photograph has to be taken.20

[16] This documentary evidence is dated 2013, well before the date when the claimant obtained his new driver's licence in XXXX 2017 (and obviously before the reforms supposedly made thereafter, according to the statement from the aforementioned business). The panel therefore concludes that the documents submitted by the claimant contain false statements fabricated to hide the fact that he was in XXXX in XXXX 2017. The panel therefore gives them no probative value and prefers the objective documentary evidence cited above, given the circumstances. Moreover, the panel concludes, in the circumstances, that the claimants are attempting to mislead the panel by alleging that they lived in hiding in XXXX and feared problems in XXXX.

[17] In this context, the panel also gives no weight to the other documents submitted by the claimants from family members and/or people they may be able to influence.21

[18] In arriving at its conclusions, the panel also took into account other concerns raised at the hearing. In each instance, the claimants gave problematic explanations that led the panel to draw negative inferences concerning the claimants' credibility as a result of these concerns. For example, the claimants stated that the people they feared had identified themselves as the Los Urabeños group. However, this group does not use this name to identify itself, but rather the name Autodefensas Gaitanistas de Colombia (AGC) [Gaitanist self-defense forces of Colombia], according to the documentary evidence.22 Invited to comment on this suspicious allegation, the claimants simply responded that that is how the person identified themself. The panel rejects this explanation, finding it improbable that a member of the AGC would identify themself that way in light of the available documentary evidence.

[19] As a second example, each of the claimants survived in extremis what they described as murder attempts. The male claimant was the first to successfully disarm and flee from an assailant who held a pistol to his head saying he would kill him. The female claimant also had a lucky escape a few months later when she, like the male claimant, was able to hit her assailant, causing him to lose his balance and the gun he had pointed at her. Moreover, the female claimant explained that, while she was fleeing, she was able to observe that her assailant had pointed his pistol at her and tried to fire more than once, but the weapon had jammed. Invited to comment on this rather unbelievable account, she explained that that is what happened, despite the fact that it was dark (the assailant was allegedly under the light of a street light) and she was running at full speed with her child in her arms to get away. The panel finds it improbable that a person fleeing imminent death with a young child in her arms would be able to see that her assailant-who was behind her and from whom she was running away-was pointing a weapon at her, pulling the trigger with his finger and then hitting his weapon as though it was damaged, all by the light of a street light. The panel does not believe the alleged incidents in the circumstances.

[20] For all these reasons,23 the panel concludes that the claimants have not credibly established their story, including the incidents alleged on and after XXXX XXXX, 2016.
Section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Act

[21] In light of its foregoing conclusion, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants have not established that they would face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or the likelihood of a risk or danger set out in subsection 97(1) of the Act.
CONCLUSION

[22] For the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" under section 96 nor "persons in need of protection" under paragraphs 97(1)(a) or (b) of the Act.

[23] Their refugee protection claims are therefore rejected.

In fact, nearly all the claimants' allegations are corroborated by documentary evidence. In addition, the factual framework contains all the necessary elements to conclude that there is a prospective risk, as well as an absence of state protection or an internal flight alternative. Faced with a file so well put together, the panel recalls the following words of a Federal Court judge:
... Evidence of a seamless web of diverse events occurring over time and distance, all intersecting propitiously and recalled with clarity and precision, should be viewed with the same caution as testimony which, by reason of multiple inconsistencies on critical issues, does not hold.3

[9] With this caution in mind, the panel sent the Minister a notice under rule 27 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules during its deliberations.4 This notice raised two concerns. First, the panel was concerned by the similarities between the claimants' story and those of claimants in other files. These similarities lay in both the basis of the narratives, in particular the systematic presence in the account of recurring elements such as murder attempts that failed as a result of exceptional circumstances, and incidents that occurred in distant cities where the claimants went to flee their problems. The Minister declined to intervene5 and the panel is therefore disregarding this concern, having chosen not to communicate the content of the other files in question and pursue the matter further.

[10] Second, the panel notified the Minister of a concern raised during the hearing, namely the presence of complaints6 in the claimants' file that are categorized as "inactivo" according to complaint reports filed through the Sistema Penal Oral Acusatorio [oral accusatory penal system] of the Fiscalia General de la Nation (FGN) [office of the attorney general].7 However, the "inactivo" status of these complaints could possibly indicate, according to responses to information requests (RIRs) produced by IRB's research services,8 that an FGN officer has determined that the crime in question did not take place.9 While the Minister also declined to intervene in this regard, the panel remains concerned by the fact that the claimants may be submitting real complaints based on fictitious facts. However, this concern does not have to do with the "inactivo" status of the complaints-the RIRs in question leave too much room for interpretation to draw a satisfactory conclusion in this regard. It also does not have to do with the authenticity of the complaints, as those submitted as evidence10 appear to be authentic. Moreover, the concern does not have to do with contradictions or omissions, as the complaints in question essentially present allegations that are consistent with each other, as well as with the claimants' story as related in the BOC Form and at the hearing. Rather, the panel is concerned about the authorities' and the complainants' follow-up to these complaints.

[11] The above-referenced RIRs report that the decision to close a complaint is usually sent to the complainant by telegram sent to the address that he or she provided. The document i) indicates that the complaint was closed and ii) provides the contact information of the FGN office where the complainant can go to learn the reasons for the decision, and iii) includes an appointment with the date and time to meet with the prosecutor. Also according to the RIRs, during the appointment, the prosecutor will produce the order closing the complaint and explain the reasons for doing so. The complainant receives a copy. In the case at hand, despite the existence of three complaints to the FGN, the only document the claimants produced in this regard is Exhibit C-31 regarding complaint D-22. However, this exhibit does not provide FGN contact information and does not inform the claimants of the possibility of obtaining more information (or even the date and time of an appointment). It also does not specify the report number assigned to the complaint-a unique number by which the complaint can be identified and traced. Moreover, its format is suspicious: the FGN logo is printed twice, one on top of the other, and covers the document date. Asked to comment, the claimants confirmed at the hearing that this document was the one they had received and referred the panel to their counsel in Colombia who was responsible for following up on all the complaints. This counsel stated in writing that the document is authentic and original and was issued by the FGN. He also explains that he met with the prosecutor responsible for the investigation and asked for it to be reopened, but the prosecutor refused because it was impossible to physically identify the perpetrators of the crime. He did not offer a copy of the decision or the order to archive the complaint, nor did he elaborate on what steps he could take to dispute the decision not to reopen the investigation. In short, he provided a vague version that does not inspire confidence in light of the aforementioned RIRs, which describe the rights and recourse available to complainants whose complaints are archived. With respect to follow-up on the other FGN complaints, counsel in Colombia is even more eager for details and essentially merely confirms their inactive status.

[12] The claimants' counsel in Canada observed that they should not be blamed for an unfamiliar legal situation regarding the status of the complaints. Whether or not these complaints are active, the claimants always followed the advice of their counsel in Colombia, who was mandated to represent them regarding their complaints and their protection. The panel informed the claimants of its concerns about the FGN complaints and gave them the time necessary to address these complaints. In the panel's opinion, the explanations contained in the two letters from counsel in Colombia11 do not satisfactorily explain the divergence between what the RIRs report about the complaint process and the situation alleged by the claimants. In light of the credibility problems outlined below, the panel is of the opinion that this divergence is better explained by the fact that the complaints were in fact made but concern fictional events, than by the claimants' version of their story being true and them relying on the good faith of their counsel in Colombia.

[13] In arriving at this conclusion, the panel also relied on the follow-up to their applications for protection made to the National Protection Unit (UNP).12 According to their Colombian counsel, he followed up in person and confirmed that the file was still being processed and that no response had been received as of XXXX XXXX, 2018. The claimants confirmed that they did not take any steps personally, again relying on their Colombian counsel. According to the documentary evidence,13 evaluation of the application by the UNP takes approximately three months and the person concerned receives a decision in writing to inform him or her of whether the application has been approved or denied, and of the protection measures that are to be implemented. In light of the documentary evidence (which presents the strengths and weaknesses of this organization and merits more weight than letters from the claimants' Colombian counsel in the circumstances), the panel finds it improbable that the claimants would have received no response or communication from the UNP in the more than 14 months since they submitted their applications. This is particularly true since the claimants were-and say they still are-reachable via the email addresses indicated on the applications. In the circumstances, the panel therefore concludes that the claimants are hiding the real outcome of their applications for protection to the UNP. This strengthens the panel's conclusion that the claimants made actual requests for protection, but on the basis of fictional facts and likely did so in order to prepare their Canadian refugee protection claims.

[14] In summary, while the panel is aware of the shortcomings in the protection Colombian authorities provide to citizens, including their capacity to investigate criminal offences, the panel is of the opinion that submitting applications for protection in Colombia triggers objective and verifiable measures that have not been demonstrated in this case, and the claimants have not been able to reasonably explain the absence of these measures. Taking into account all the credibility problems noted below, the panel concludes that the claimants have manipulated the Colombian protection system by submitting actual complaints based on fictitious events. It therefore gives no evidentiary weight to the measures taken by the claimants with the Colombian authorities.

[15] Another element undermining the claimants' credibility: their alleged stay of several months in XXXX while fleeing their alleged problems in XXXX. The panel questioned the claimants at length about this stay, given that they allegedly arrived in this city, over 300 kilometres from XXXX, with the intention of rebuilding their life. Living in a new city requires actions that leave traces and that can be documented, beyond the exhibits submitted in evidence prior to the hearing and pertinent to this stay.14 Without going into details, the panel observed that all the evidence submitted (before and after15 the hearing) in this regard is documents it gives no evidentiary weight to in the circumstances, given that they come from sources controlled by the claimants, that they are easy to fabricate or that they present inconsistencies.16 The claimants could not produce any documents that might have merited evidentiary weight (e.g., confirmations of bank transfers that the claimants allegedly received in XXXX from their parents or their own bank statements reflecting ATM withdrawals in XXXX or purchases they allegedly made from businesses in the city). On one hand, they did not keep them (even though they fortuitously kept a hotel invoice and a transportation ticket); on the other hand, efforts to obtain them since have been unsuccessful.17 Rather than elaborate on whether or not these efforts and explanations for the lack of independent evidence to corroborate the claimants' alleged stay in XXXX are reasonable, the panel will turn to a more determinative element, namely the fact that the male claimant was issued a new driver's licence in XXXX during this alleged stay. The male claimant explained that he did not go to the national capital in person to get this document (nor to any other government institution in the country), but that, instead, his father had done so on his behalf. Confronted with the fact that his own presence is required for this according to the documentary evidence,18 the claimant stated that he had never returned to XXXX and that his father had taken the necessary steps. In support of this argument, he used the extension granted by the panel to submit documents after the hearing,19 including a letter from himself asking his father to do this, a statement from his father and a statement from a business indicating that [translation] "it was possible to renew a driver's licence without the presence of the licence-holder via an authorization and with the documents mentioned above, but it is no longer possible after the latest reforms." Note that the male claimant did not produce [translation] "independent and objective" documents from the authorities responsible for issuing driver's licences confirming the possibility of having a driver's licence issued in the circumstances alleged in XXXX 2017. Nor did he submit "independent and objective" documents supporting "the latest reforms" mentioned in the statement from the aforementioned business or the date of these reforms. Moreover, the aforementioned documentary evidence states the following:
Sources indicate that driver's licences for personal vehicles are valid indefinitely. However, the website of the Ministry of Transportation indicates that the holder has to undergo a professional medical exam every six years to prove his or her mental and physical suitability to drive a personal vehicle.
Two sources indicated that a driver's licence can be obtained only in person. The representative of the Secretariat of Transportation and Traffic of XXXX explained that it has to be done in person because an individual has to be fingerprinted and his or her photograph has to be taken.20

[16] This documentary evidence is dated 2013, well before the date when the claimant obtained his new driver's licence in XXXX 2017 (and obviously before the reforms supposedly made thereafter, according to the statement from the aforementioned business). The panel therefore concludes that the documents submitted by the claimant contain false statements fabricated to hide the fact that he was in XXXX in XXXX 2017. The panel therefore gives them no probative value and prefers the objective documentary evidence cited above, given the circumstances. Moreover, the panel concludes, in the circumstances, that the claimants are attempting to mislead the panel by alleging that they lived in hiding in XXXX and feared problems in XXXX.
[17] In this context, the panel also gives no weight to the other documents submitted by the claimants from family members and/or people they may be able to influence.21

[18] In arriving at its conclusions, the panel also took into account other concerns raised at the hearing. In each instance, the claimants gave problematic explanations that led the panel to draw negative inferences concerning the claimants' credibility as a result of these concerns. For example, the claimants stated that the people they feared had identified themselves as the Los Urabeños group. However, this group does not use this name to identify itself, but rather the name Autodefensas Gaitanistas de Colombia (AGC) [Gaitanist self-defense forces of Colombia], according to the documentary evidence.22 Invited to comment on this suspicious allegation, the claimants simply responded that that is how the person identified themself. The panel rejects this explanation, finding it improbable that a member of the AGC would identify themself that way in light of the available documentary evidence.

[19] As a second example, each of the claimants survived in extremis what they described as murder attempts. The male claimant was the first to successfully disarm and flee from an assailant who held a pistol to his head saying he would kill him. The female claimant also had a lucky escape a few months later when she, like the male claimant, was able to hit her assailant, causing him to lose his balance and the gun he had pointed at her. Moreover, the female claimant explained that, while she was fleeing, she was able to observe that her assailant had pointed his pistol at her and tried to fire more than once, but the weapon had jammed. Invited to comment on this rather unbelievable account, she explained that that is what happened, despite the fact that it was dark (the assailant was allegedly under the light of a street light) and she was running at full speed with her child in her arms to get away. The panel finds it improbable that a person fleeing imminent death with a young child in her arms would be able to see that her assailant-who was behind her and from whom she was running away-was pointing a weapon at her, pulling the trigger with his finger and then hitting his weapon as though it was damaged, all by the light of a street light. The panel does not believe the alleged incidents in the circumstances.

[20] For all these reasons,23 the panel concludes that the claimants have not credibly established their story, including the incidents alleged on and after XXXX XXXX, 2016.
Section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Act

[21] In light of its foregoing conclusion, the panel is of the opinion that the claimants have not established that they would face a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or the likelihood of a risk or danger set out in subsection 97(1) of the Act.
CONCLUSION

[22] For the foregoing reasons, the panel determines that the claimants are neither "Convention refugees" under section 96 nor "persons in need of protection" under paragraphs 97(1)(a) or (b) of the Act.

[23] Their refugee protection claims are therefore rejected.
